From an Amazon review:

SPOILERS) I can offer no more genuine recommendation for this book than to observe that it changed my mind on an issue I felt strongly about. Specifically, based on what I read and heard about the murder of Matthew Shepard in 1998, the media's confident portrayal of the circumstances and motive of that murder had convinced me that "the people of Wyoming" were barbaric bigots. After reading Stephen Jimenez' doggedly investigated book The Story of Matt: Hidden Truths About the Murder of Matthew Shepard, I now realize that events leading to Matthew's Shepard's murder were much more complex than portrayed in the media and that the motivation for the attack was so simplified in the media that it became a misleading untruth. This conclusion made me realize that my own opinions about "the people of Wyoming," based on this media coverage, were as bigoted as those I presumed to judge. So I changed my mind about "the people of Wyoming." Are there bigots in Wyoming? I'm sure there are. But there are bigots everywhere. I have to relearn to observe from a perspective that I thought was a core belief. People should be judged as individuals on merit.

Turning to the book itself, I found it as compelling as Truman Capote's In Cold Blood. During my reading I also found myself thinking of similarities to David Lynch's iconic movie Blue Velvet and the seamy underside of the meth culture portrayed in Breaking Bad. Jimenez, a journalist, explains in the Author's Note why he decided to look further into Matthew's murder. Eventually his investigation would continue for almost 15 years. The duration of the investigation eventually added clarity as various individuals who percieved they had "something to hide" in the immediate aftermath of the murder and trial felt less threatened over time and provided "additional details." The book was published in 2013.

As in reconstruction of any complex event, there are no easy answers here. Contradictory statements, sometimes by the same peron at different times, contradictory documents, opinions express, issues avoided, deliberate deceit, inconsistencies, etc. frustrate the search for accuracy. Jimenez sometimes offers possible explainations for such issues but certainty is unachievable. The reader must decide who and what seems credible and what does not. The list of sources at the end is meant in a journalistic sense i.e. a list of persons the author got information from during his investigation. This is investigative journalism, not history researched to the standards of academic credibility. Nor is it evidence presented according to the requirements of criminal law.

The first section of the book provides a wide-ranging examination, through interviews, case and court records, of Matthew, his murders, their friends and acquaintainces, law enforcement, prosecutors, lawyers and anyone else Jimenez thought could shed light on the case. Jimenez had access to all the investigation documents, the trial records, and previously sealed documents and evidence. He was encouraged by Albany County Wyoming Attorney Cal Rerucha who prosecuted of Matthew's murders. Rerucha had come to have doubts about whether the trial had accurately captured all the relevant aspects of the case.

The second section of the book is a painstaking reconstruction of the days before the attack, the day of the attack, the attack itself, the hours and days following the attack leading to the suspects arrest and initial interrogation, the growing media and public awareness of the story, reactions of Matthew's friends and family, Matthew's medical treatment, Matthew's death 6 days after the attack, and the subsequent course of the investigation until the opening of Russell Henderson's trial in March 1999.

The third section of the book is about the opening of Russell Henderson's trial, and the considerations and negations for Henderson's plea bargain that obviated that trial, along with Henderson's sentencing hearing.

The fourth part is about the trial and sentencing of Aaron McKinney in the Fall of 1999, information that came to Jimenez attention years later, and the search for reconciliation between Matthew's longtime friend Ted Hensen and Russell Henderson, who is serving two life terms for Matthew's murder..

An Epilogue speaks briefly of Jimenez' sense of closure on such a lengthy investigation during his last visit to Wyoming related to writing the book in April 2013.

Not surprisingly, this book has attracted controversy. If you search Wikipedia for Matthew Shepard and scroll to the bottom you will find a paragraph about the book's criticism. I came across that in the middle of Jimenez' book. I read nothing there that I felt merited further examination. In an Afterward to The Book of Matt, Jimenez addresses the book's critics directly and, in my view, convincingly. For those considering reading Jimenez' book, I recommend finding the book in a store or library and reading the Author's Note in the beginning and the Epilogue and Afterward before making your decision.

In the Afterword, Jimenez quotes Aaron Hicklin, editor and chief of Out Magazine in his review of The Book of Matt for The Advocate magazine: “There are obvious reasons why advocates of hate crime legislation must want to preserve one particular version of the Matthew Shepard story, but it was always just that —a version. Jimenez’s version is another, more studiously reported account … Whether it was a hate crime, a drug crime, or a combination of the two, it’s hard to shake the suspicion that self-hate and a misguided culture of masculinity, which taught McKinney to abhor in himself what Shepard had learned to embrace, was as complicit as anything else in the murder of Matthew Shepard. That is, of course, a kind of hate crime —just not as straightforward as the one we’ve embraced all these years.”

In addition to correcting my own misinformed opinion about "the people of Wyoming," the book fascinates me by documenting the process by which a dramatic historic event is transformed into a larger-than-life seminal event in our national conscience and a milestone in American History. The murder of Matthew Shepard is such an event. This book is not about changing or discounting the understanding of Matthew's brutal murder as 1) a milestone of the American History 2) a catalyst for raising awareness of hate crimes 3) motivation for clarification of the legal definition of "hate crime" 4) motivation for passage of hate crime legislation on the national and state level 5) nor as an important contribution in the GLBT struggle for social justice.
